**Robert Gabriel Mugabe**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-3) (21 February 1924 – 6 September 2019) was a Zimbabwean revolutionary, politician, and dictator who led [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe") from 1980 until 2017. He served as the country's first [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Zimbabwe "Prime Minister of Zimbabwe") from 1980 to 1987 and as its second [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Zimbabwe "President of Zimbabwe") from 1987 to 2017. He also led the [Zimbabwe African National Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Union "Zimbabwe African National Union") (ZANU) from 1975 to 1980 and then its successor political party, the [ZANU – Patriotic Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZANU%E2%80%93PF "ZANU–PF") (ZANU–PF), from 1980 to 2017. Ideologically an [African nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_nationalist "African nationalist"), during the 1970s and 1980s he identified as a [Marxist–Leninist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxist%E2%80%93Leninist "Marxist–Leninist"), and from the 1990s as a [socialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist "Socialist").

Mugabe was born to a poor [Shona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shona_people "Shona people") family in [Kutama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kutama,_Zimbabwe "Kutama, Zimbabwe"), [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia"). Educated at [Kutama College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kutama_College "Kutama College") and the [University of Fort Hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Fort_Hare "University of Fort Hare"), he worked as a schoolteacher. Angered by [white minority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_people_in_Zimbabwe "White people in Zimbabwe") rule of his homeland within the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire"), Mugabe embraced [Marxism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxism "Marxism") and joined African nationalists calling for an independent state controlled by the black majority. After making antigovernmental comments, he was convicted of [sedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedition "Sedition") and imprisoned between 1964 and 1974. On release, he fled to Mozambique, established his leadership of ZANU, and oversaw its role in the [Rhodesian Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War"), fighting [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith")'s predominantly white government. He reluctantly participated in peace talks in the United Kingdom that resulted in the [Lancaster House Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House_Agreement "Lancaster House Agreement"), ending the war. In the [1980 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Southern_Rhodesian_general_election "1980 Southern Rhodesian general election"), Mugabe led ZANU-PF to victory, becoming prime minister when the country, now renamed Zimbabwe, gained internationally recognised independence later that year. Mugabe's administration expanded healthcare and [education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education "Education") and—despite his professed desire for a [socialist society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_mode_of_production "Socialist mode of production")—adhered largely to [mainstream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainstream_economics "Mainstream economics") economic policies.

Mugabe's calls for racial reconciliation failed to stem growing white emigration, while relations with [Joshua Nkomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Nkomo "Joshua Nkomo")'s [Zimbabwe African People's Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_People's_Union "Zimbabwe African People's Union") (ZAPU) also deteriorated. In the [Gukurahundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gukurahundi "Gukurahundi") of 1982–1987, Mugabe's [5th Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5th_Brigade_(Zimbabwe) "5th Brigade (Zimbabwe)") crushed ZAPU-linked opposition in [Matabeleland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matabeleland "Matabeleland") in a campaign that killed at least 20,000 people. Internationally, he sent troops into the [Second Congo War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Congo_War "Second Congo War") and chaired the [Non-Aligned Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement "Non-Aligned Movement") (1986–1989), the [Organisation of African Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_African_Unity "Organisation of African Unity") (1997–1998), and the [African Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Union "African Union") (2015–2016). Pursuing [decolonisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation "Decolonisation"), Mugabe emphasised the [redistribution of land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reform_in_Zimbabwe "Land reform in Zimbabwe") controlled by white farmers to landless blacks; from 2000 he encouraged black Zimbabweans to violently seize white-owned farms. Food production was severely impacted, leading to famine, hyperinflation, economic decline, and foreign sanctions. Opposition to Mugabe grew, but he was re-elected in [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Zimbabwean_presidential_election "2002 Zimbabwean presidential election"), [2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Zimbabwean_general_election "2008 Zimbabwean general election"), and [2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Zimbabwean_general_election "2013 Zimbabwean general election") through campaigns dominated by violence, [electoral fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_fraud "Electoral fraud"), and nationalistic appeals to his rural Shona voter base. In 2017, members of his party [ousted him in a coup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Zimbabwean_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "2017 Zimbabwean coup d'état"), replacing him with former vice president [Emmerson Mnangagwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmerson_Mnangagwa "Emmerson Mnangagwa"). Mugabe died in [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore") two years later.

Having dominated Zimbabwe's politics for nearly four decades, Mugabe was a controversial figure. He was praised as a revolutionary hero of the African liberation struggle who helped free Zimbabwe from British [colonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonialism "Colonialism"), [imperialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperialism "Imperialism"), and white minority rule. Critics accused Mugabe of being a dictator responsible for [economic mismanagement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe "Hyperinflation in Zimbabwe") and widespread [corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption_in_Zimbabwe "Corruption in Zimbabwe") and [human rights abuses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_Zimbabwe "Human rights in Zimbabwe"), including [anti-white racism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism_in_Zimbabwe "Racism in Zimbabwe"), [crimes against humanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimes_against_humanity "Crimes against humanity"), and genocide.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Mugabe&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

### Childhood: 1924–1945

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Mugabe&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Childhood: 1924–1945")]

Robert Gabriel Mugabe was born on 21 February 1924 at the [Kutama Mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kutama,_Zimbabwe "Kutama, Zimbabwe") village in [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia")'s [Lomagundi District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lomagundi_District "Lomagundi District") (in an area that is now part of [Zvimba District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zvimba_District "Zvimba District")) in [Mashonaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashonaland "Mashonaland").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200217Meredith200219-4) His father, Gabriel Matibiri, was a carpenter, while his mother Bona was a Christian [catechist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catechist "Catechist") for the village children.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198111Blair200217Meredith200219,_21Norman200815-5) Bona and Gabriel had six children: Miteri (Michael), Raphael, Robert, Dhonandhe (Donald), [Sabina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabina_Mugabe "Sabina Mugabe"), and Bridgette.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198111Blair200217-6) They belonged to the Zezuru clan, one of the smallest branches of the [Shona people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shona_people "Shona people").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200226-7) Mugabe's paternal grandfather was [Chief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chieftain "Chieftain") Constantine Karigamombe, alias "Matibiri", a powerful figure who served King [Lobengula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobengula "Lobengula") in the 19th century.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-8) Through his father, he claimed membership of the [chieftaincy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chieftaincy "Chieftaincy") family that has provided the hereditary rulers of Zvimba for generations.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-9)

The Jesuits were strict disciplinarians and under their influence Mugabe developed an intense self-discipline,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200219-10) while also becoming a devout Catholic.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolland20083-11) Mugabe excelled at school,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200218-12) where he was a secretive and solitary child,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200218Meredith200220-13) preferring to read, rather than playing sports or socialising with other children.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200218Meredith200220%E2%80%9321-14) He was taunted by many of the other children, who regarded him as a coward and a [mother's boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother's_boy "Mother's boy").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolland20086%E2%80%937-15)

In about 1930 Gabriel had an argument with one of the Jesuits, and as a result the Mugabe family was expelled from the mission village by its French leader, Father Jean-Baptiste Loubière.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200217%E2%80%9318-16) The family settled in a village about 11 kilometres (7 miles) away; the children were permitted to remain at the mission primary school, living with relatives in Kutama during term-time and returning to their parental home on weekends.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200218-12) Around the same time, Robert's older brother Raphael died, likely of [diarrhoea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diarrhoea "Diarrhoea").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200218-12) In early 1934, Robert's other older brother, Michael, also died, after consuming poisoned maize.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198111Blair200218Holland2008224-17) Later that year, Gabriel left his family in search of employment in [Bulawayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulawayo "Bulawayo").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200218Meredith200221Norman200815-18) He subsequently abandoned Bona and their six children and established a relationship with another woman, with whom he had three further offspring.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200221-19)

Loubière died shortly after and was replaced by an Irishman, Father Jerome O'Hea, who welcomed the return of the Mugabe family to Kutama.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200218-12) In contrast to the racism that permeated Southern Rhodesian society, under O'Hea's leadership the Kutama Mission preached an ethos of racial equality.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198115Norman200816-20) O'Hea nurtured the young Mugabe; shortly before his death in 1970 he described the latter as having "an exceptional mind and an exceptional heart".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198112Blair200218Norman200816-21) As well as helping provide Mugabe with a Christian education, O'Hea taught him about the [Irish War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_War_of_Independence "Irish War of Independence"), in which [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Free_State "Irish Free State") had seceded from the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200221Norman200816-22) After completing six years of elementary education, in 1941 Mugabe was offered a place on a teacher training course at [Kutama College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kutama_College "Kutama College"). Mugabe's mother could not afford the tuition fees, which were paid in part by his grandfather and in part by O'Hea.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198114Blair200218Meredith200221Norman200816-23) As part of this education, Mugabe began teaching at his old school, earning £2 per month, which he used to support his family.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200218Norman200816-24) In 1944, Gabriel returned to Kutama with his three new children, but died shortly after, leaving Robert to take financial responsibility for both his three siblings and three half-siblings.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200218Norman200816-24) Having attained a teaching diploma, Mugabe left Kutama in 1945.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200222-25)

### University education and teaching career: 1945–1960

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Mugabe&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: University education and teaching career: 1945–1960")]

During the following years, Mugabe taught at various schools around Southern Rhodesia,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198116Blair200219Meredith200222-26) among them the Dadaya Mission school in [Shabani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zvishavane "Zvishavane").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198116Norman200816%E2%80%9317-27) There is no evidence that Mugabe was involved in political activity at the time, and he did not participate in the country's [1948 general strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_in_Southern_Rhodesia "1948 in Southern Rhodesia").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200219-28) In 1949 he won a scholarship to study at the [University of Fort Hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Fort_Hare "University of Fort Hare") in South Africa's [Eastern Cape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Cape "Eastern Cape").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198116Blair200219Meredith200222Norman200817-29) There he joined the [African National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_National_Congress "African National Congress") youth league (ANCYL)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198117Norman200817-30) and attended [African nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_nationalist "African nationalist") meetings, where he met a number of Jewish South African [communists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communists "Communists") who introduced him to [Marxist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxist "Marxist") ideas.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198116Meredith200222-31) He later related that despite this exposure to Marxism, his biggest influence at the time were the actions of [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi") during the [Indian independence movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_independence_movement "Indian independence movement").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198117Meredith200222%E2%80%9323-32) In 1952, he left the university with a Bachelor of Arts degree in history and English literature.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200219Norman200817-33) In later years he described his time at Fort Hare as the "turning point" in his life.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198117-34)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Kwame_Nkrumah_%28JFKWHP-AR6409-A%29.jpg/250px-Kwame_Nkrumah_%28JFKWHP-AR6409-A%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kwame_Nkrumah_(JFKWHP-AR6409-A).jpg)

Mugabe was inspired by the example set by Ghana's [Kwame Nkrumah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah "Kwame Nkrumah").

Mugabe returned to Southern Rhodesia in 1952,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200219Meredith200223-35) by which time—he later related— he was "completely hostile to the [colonialist] system".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200223-36) Here, his first job was as a teacher at the Driefontein Catholic Mission School near [Umvuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mvuma "Mvuma").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198117Norman200817-30) In 1953 he relocated to the Highfield Government School in [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare")'s [Harari township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mbare "Mbare") and in 1954 to the Mambo Township Government School in [Gwelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwelo "Gwelo").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorman200817-37) Meanwhile, he gained a [Bachelor of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Education "Bachelor of Education") degree by correspondence from the [University of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_South_Africa "University of South Africa"),[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200223Norman200817-38) and ordered a number of Marxist tracts—among them [Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx "Karl Marx")'s _[Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital:\_Critique\_of\_Political\_Economy "Capital: Critique of Political Economy")_ and [Friedrich Engels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Engels "Friedrich Engels")' _[The Condition of the Working Class in England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Condition\_of\_the\_Working\_Class\_in\_England "The Condition of the Working Class in England")_—from a London mail-order company.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198118Meredith200223-39) Despite his growing interest in politics, he was not active in any political movement.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200223-36) He joined a number of inter-racial groups, such as the [Capricorn Africa Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capricorn_Africa_Society "Capricorn Africa Society"), through which he mixed with both black and white Rhodesians.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198118%E2%80%9319-40)[Guy Clutton-Brock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Clutton-Brock "Guy Clutton-Brock"), who knew Mugabe through this group, later noted that he was "an extraordinary young man" who could be "a bit of a cold fish at times" but "could talk about [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley "Elvis Presley") or [Bing Crosby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bing_Crosby "Bing Crosby") as easily as politics".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198119Blair200218%E2%80%9319-41)

From 1955 to 1958, Mugabe lived in neighbouring [Northern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Rhodesia "Northern Rhodesia"), where he worked at Chalimbana Teacher Training College in [Lusaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusaka "Lusaka").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200223Norman200817-38) There he continued his education by working on a second degree by correspondence, this time a Bachelor of Administration from the [University of London International Programmes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London_International_Programmes "University of London International Programmes") through [distance learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance_learning "Distance learning").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200223Norman200817-38) In Northern Rhodesia, he was taken in for a time by the family of [Emmerson Mnangagwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmerson_Mnangagwa "Emmerson Mnangagwa"), whom Mugabe inspired to join the liberation movement and who would later go on to be [President of Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Zimbabwe "President of Zimbabwe").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-:8-42) In 1958, Mugabe moved to Ghana to work at St Mary's Teacher Training College in [Takoradi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takoradi "Takoradi").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198121Blair200219Meredith200223-43) He taught at Apowa Secondary School, also at Takoradi, after obtaining his local certification at [Achimota College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achimota_College "Achimota College") (1958–1960), where he met his first wife, [Sally Hayfron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Hayfron "Sally Hayfron").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-44) According to Mugabe, "I went [to Ghana] as an adventurist. I wanted to see what it would be like in an independent African state".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198122-45) Ghana had been the first African state to gain independence from European colonial powers and under the leadership of [Kwame Nkrumah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah "Kwame Nkrumah") underwent a range of African nationalist reforms; Mugabe reveled in this environment.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198121Blair200219Meredith200223%E2%80%9324-46) In tandem with his teaching, Mugabe attended the [Kwame Nkrumah Ideological Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah_Ideological_Institute "Kwame Nkrumah Ideological Institute") in [Winneba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winneba "Winneba").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorman200818Ndlovu-Gatsheni20091142-47) Mugabe later claimed that it was in Ghana that he finally embraced Marxism.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198122Blair200219Meredith200224Norman200818-48) He also began a relationship there with Hayfron who worked at the college and shared his political interests.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198122Meredith200224Holland200811%E2%80%9312Norman200817-49)

## Revolutionary activity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Mugabe&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Revolutionary activity")]

### Early political career: 1960–1963

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Mugabe&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Early political career: 1960–1963")]

While Mugabe was teaching abroad, an anti-colonialist African nationalist movement was established in Southern Rhodesia. It was first led by [Joshua Nkomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Nkomo "Joshua Nkomo")'s [Southern Rhodesia African National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_African_National_Congress "Southern Rhodesia African National Congress"), founded in September 1957 and then banned by the colonial government in February 1959.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198133%E2%80%9334Meredith200224%E2%80%9325-50) SRANC was replaced by the more radically oriented [National Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Democratic_Party_(Southern_Rhodesia) "National Democratic Party (Southern Rhodesia)") (NDP), founded in January 1960.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198135Meredith200226-51) In May 1960, Mugabe returned to Southern Rhodesia, bringing Hayfron with him.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198124Meredith200226-52) The pair had planned for their visit to be short, however Mugabe's friend, the African nationalist [Leopold Takawira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopold_Takawira "Leopold Takawira"), urged them to stay.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200226-53)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Joshua_Nkomo_%281978%29.jpg/250px-Joshua_Nkomo_%281978%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Joshua_Nkomo_(1978).jpg)

[Joshua Nkomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Nkomo "Joshua Nkomo") became one of the leading figures of resistance to white minority rule in Southern Rhodesia.

In July 1960, Takawira and two other NDP officials were arrested; in protest, Mugabe joined a demonstration of 7,000 people who planned to march from [Highfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highfield,_Zimbabwe "Highfield, Zimbabwe") to the Prime Minister's office in Salisbury. The demonstration was stopped by riot police outside Stoddart Hall in Harare township.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198125%E2%80%9326Meredith200226Norman200843-54) By midday the next day, the crowd had grown to 40,000 and a makeshift platform had been erected for speakers. Having become a much-respected figure through his profession, his possession of three degrees, and his travels abroad, Mugabe was among those invited to speak to the crowd.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198127Meredith200226Holland200813-55) Following this event, Mugabe decided to devote himself full-time to activism, resigning his teaching post in Ghana (after having served two years of the four-year teaching contract).[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200227-56) He chaired the first NDP congress, held in October 1960, assisted by [Herbert Chitepo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Chitepo "Herbert Chitepo") on the procedural aspects. Mugabe was elected the party's publicity secretary.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198137Meredith200227Norman200844-57) Mugabe consciously injected emotionalism into the NDP's African nationalism, hoping to broaden its support among the wider population by appealing to traditional cultural values.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198137-58) He helped to form the NDP Youth Wing and encouraged the incorporation of ancestral prayers, traditional costume, and female [ululation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ululation "Ululation") into its meetings.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198137%E2%80%9338-59) In February 1961 he married Hayfron in a Catholic ceremony conducted in Salisbury; she had converted to Catholicism to make this possible.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198138Blair200220Meredith200227Holland200813Norman200844-60)

The British government held a Salisbury conference in 1961 to determine Southern Rhodesia's future. Nkomo led an NDP delegation, which hoped that the British would support the creation of an independent state governed by the black majority. Representatives of the country's white minority—who then controlled Southern Rhodesia's government—were opposed to this, promoting continued white minority rule.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200227%E2%80%9328-61) Following negotiations, Nkomo agreed to a proposal which would allow the black population representation through 15 of the 65 seats in the country's parliament. Mugabe and others in the NDP were furious at Nkomo's compromise.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198139%E2%80%9340Meredith200228-62) Following the conference, Southern Rhodesia's African nationalist movement fell into disarray.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200228-63) Mugabe spoke at a number of NDP rallies before the party was banned by the government in December 1961.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198142Meredith200229Norman200844-64) Many of its members re-grouped as the [Zimbabwe African People's Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_People's_Union "Zimbabwe African People's Union") (ZAPU) several days later,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198143Meredith200229Norman200844-65) with Mugabe appointed as ZAPU's publicity secretary and general secretary.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorman200844-66)

Racial violence was growing in the country, with aggrieved black Africans targeting the white community.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200229-67) Mugabe deemed such conflict a necessary tactic in the overthrow of British colonial dominance and white minority rule. This contrasted with Nkomo's view that African nationalists should focus on international diplomacy to encourage the British government to grant their demands.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200229-67) Nine months after it had been founded, ZAPU was also banned by the government,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198143Meredith200229Norman200844-65) and in September 1962 Mugabe and other senior party officials were arrested and restricted to their home districts for three months.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198143Meredith200229Norman200844-65) Both Mugabe and his wife were in trouble with the law; he had been charged with making subversive statements in a public speech and awarded bail before his trial.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198145Meredith200231-68) Hayfron had been sentenced to two years imprisonment—suspended for 15 months—for a speech in which she declared that the British Queen [Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II") "can go to hell".[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198145%E2%80%9346Meredith200231-69)

> Europeans must realise that unless the legitimate demands of African nationalism are recognised, then racial conflict is inevitable.

—Mugabe, early 1960s[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198142Norman200844-70)

The rise of African nationalism generated a white backlash in Southern Rhodesia, with the right-wing [Rhodesian Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Front "Rhodesian Front") winning the [December 1962 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_Southern_Rhodesian_general_election "1962 Southern Rhodesian general election"). The new government sought to preserve white minority rule by tightening security and establishing full independence from the United Kingdom.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198145Meredith200230-71) Mugabe met with colleagues at his house in Salisbury's Highbury district, where he argued that as political demonstrations were simply being banned, it was time to move towards armed resistance.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200230-72) Both he and others rejected Nkomo's proposal that they establish a government-in-exile in [Dar es Salaam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dar_es_Salaam "Dar es Salaam").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198144%E2%80%9345Meredith200230%E2%80%9331-73) He and Hayfron skipped bail to attend a ZAPU meeting in the [Tanganyikan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanganyika_(1961%E2%80%931964) "Tanganyika (1961–1964)") city.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198146%E2%80%9347Meredith200231-74) There, the party leadership met Tanganyika's president, [Julius Nyerere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Nyerere "Julius Nyerere"), who also dismissed the idea of a government-in-exile and urged ZAPU to organise their resistance to white minority rule within Southern Rhodesia itself.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198147Meredith200231-75)

In August, Hayfron gave birth to Mugabe's son, whom they named Nhamodzenyika, a Shona term meaning "suffering country".[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198148Blair200220Meredith200232Holland200814Norman200845-76) Mugabe insisted that she take their son back to Ghana, while he decided to return to Southern Rhodesia.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198149Meredith200232-77) There, African nationalists opposed to Nkomo's leadership had established a new party, the [Zimbabwe African National Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Union "Zimbabwe African National Union") (ZANU), in August; [Ndabaningi Sithole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ndabaningi_Sithole "Ndabaningi Sithole") became the group's president, while appointing Mugabe to be the group's secretary-general _in absentia_.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198149Meredith200232Norman200846-78) Nkomo responded by forming his own group, the People's Caretaker Council, which was widely referred to as "ZAPU" after its predecessor.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200232-79) ZAPU and ZANU violently opposed one another and soon gang warfare broke out between their rival memberships.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200233-80)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-struggleforzimbabwe7071-81)

### Imprisonment: 1963–1974

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Mugabe&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Imprisonment: 1963–1974")]

Mugabe was arrested on his return to Southern Rhodesia in December 1963.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198149Blair200221Meredith200233Norman200849-82) His trial lasted from January to March 1964, during which he refused to retract the subversive statements that he had publicly made.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198149Meredith200233-83) In March 1964 he was sentenced to 21 months' imprisonment.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200233-80) Mugabe was first imprisoned at Salisbury Maximum Security Prison, before being moved to the [Wha Wha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Prison_Service "Rhodesia Prison Service") detention centre and then the Sikombela detention centre in [Que Que](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Que_Que "Que Que").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198151Blair200221Meredith200233%E2%80%9334Norman200850-84) At the latter, he organised study classes for the inmates, teaching them basic literacy, maths, and English.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198154Meredith200234Holland200827Norman200851-85) Sympathetic black warders smuggled messages from Mugabe and other members of the ZANU executive committee to activists outside the prison.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198155-86) At the executive's bidding, ZANU activist [Herbert Chitepo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Chitepo "Herbert Chitepo") had organised a small guerrilla force in [Lusaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusaka "Lusaka"). In April 1966 the group carried out a failed attempt to destroy power pylons at [Sinoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinoia "Sinoia"), and shortly after attacked a white-owned farm near [Hartley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chegutu "Chegutu"), killing its inhabitants.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198155%E2%80%9356-87) The government responded by returning the members of the ZANU executive, including Mugabe, to Salisbury Prison in 1966.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198155Meredith200234-88) There, forty prisoners were divided among four communal cells, with many sleeping on the concrete floor due to overcrowding;[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198156-89) Mugabe shared his cell with Sithole, [Enos Nkala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enos_Nkala "Enos Nkala"), and [Edgar Tekere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Tekere "Edgar Tekere").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200234-90) He remained there for eight years, devoting his time to reading and studying.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200234-90) During this period, he gained several further degrees from the University of London: a masters in economics, a bachelor of administration, and two law degrees.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200222Meredith200234-91)

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6c/Ian_Smith_1975.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ian_Smith_1975.jpg)

While Mugabe was imprisoned, [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith") became leader of Rhodesia.

While imprisoned, Mugabe learned that his son had died of [encephalitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encephalitis "Encephalitis") at the age of three. Mugabe was grief-stricken and requested a leave of absence to visit his wife in Ghana. He never forgave the prison authorities for refusing this request.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198157%E2%80%9358Blair200221%E2%80%9322Meredith200234%E2%80%9335Holland200827%E2%80%9328-92) Claims have also circulated among those who knew him at the time that Mugabe was subjected to both physical and mental torture during his imprisonment.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolland2008158-93) According to Father Emmanuel Ribeiro, who was Mugabe's priest during his imprisonment, Mugabe got through the experience "partly through the strength of his spirituality" but also because his "real strength was study and helping others to learn".[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolland2008152-94)

While Mugabe was imprisoned, in August 1964, the Rhodesian Front government—now under the leadership of [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith")—banned ZANU and ZAPU and arrested all remaining leaders of the country's African nationalist movement.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200233Norman200851-95) Smith's government made a [unilateral declaration of independence from the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia's_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence") in November 1965, renaming Southern Rhodesia as Rhodesia; the UK refused to recognise the legitimacy of this and imposed economic sanctions on the country.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198155Blair200221Meredith200235%E2%80%9336Norman200854-96)

In 1972, the African nationalists launched a guerrilla war against Smith's government.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200223Meredith200236%E2%80%9337-97) Among the revolutionaries, it was known as the "Second Chimurenga".[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200223Alao201221-98) Paramilitary groups based themselves in neighboring Tanzania and Zambia; many of their fighters were inadequately armed and trained.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198161-99) ZANU's military wing, the [Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Liberation_Army "Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army") (ZANLA), consisted largely of Shona. It was based in neighboring [Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Mozambique "People's Republic of Mozambique") and gained funds from the People's Republic of China. ZAPU's military wing, the [Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_People's_Revolutionary_Army "Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army") (ZIPRA), was instead funded by the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"), was based in Zambia, and consisted largely of [Ndebele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ndebele_people "Northern Ndebele people").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200223Meredith200236%E2%80%9337Alao201220-100)

Mugabe and other senior ZANU members had growing doubts about Sithole's leadership, deeming him increasingly irritable and irrational.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198166-101) In October 1968 Sithole had tried to smuggle a message out of the prison commanding ZANU activists to assassinate Smith. His plan was discovered, and he was put on trial in January 1969; desperate to avoid a death sentence, he declared that he renounced violence and his previous ideological commitments.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198166%E2%80%9368Norman200855-102) Mugabe denounced Sithole's "treachery" in rejecting ZANU's cause, and the executive removed him as ZANU President in a [vote of no confidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vote_of_no_confidence "Vote of no confidence"), selecting Mugabe as his successor.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198168Blair200222Norman200856-103) In November 1974, the ZANU executive voted to suspend Sithole's membership of the organization.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198172Norman200857-104)

Fearing that the guerrilla war would spread south, the South African government pressured Rhodesia to advance the process of détente with the politically moderate black governments of Zambia and Tanzania. As part of these negotiations, Smith's government agreed to release a number of black revolutionaries who had been indefinitely detained.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200222Norman200857-105) After almost eleven years of imprisonment, Mugabe was released in November 1974.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200222Meredith200237Norman200859-106) He moved in with his sister Sabina at her home in Highfield township.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200222-107) He was intent on joining the ZANU forces and taking part in the guerrilla war,[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200237-108) recognising that to secure dominance of ZANU he would have to take command of ZANLA.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200223-109) This was complicated by internal violence within the paramilitary group, predominately between members of the [Manyika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manyika "Manyika") and [Karange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karange?action=edit&redlink=1 "Karange (page does not exist)") groups of Shona.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198176%E2%80%9378-110)

### Guerrilla war: 1975–1979

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Mugabe&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Guerrilla war: 1975–1979")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Flag_of_ZANU-PF.svg/250px-Flag_of_ZANU-PF.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_ZANU-PF.svg)

The flag of the [Zimbabwe African National Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Union "Zimbabwe African National Union") (ZANU)

In March 1975, Mugabe resolved to leave Rhodesia for Mozambique, ambitious to take control of ZANU's guerrilla campaign.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith20024-111) After his friend [Maurice Nyagumbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Nyagumbo "Maurice Nyagumbo") was arrested, he feared the same fate but was hidden from the authorities by Ribeiro. Ribeiro and a sympathetic nun then assisted him and [Edgar Tekere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Tekere "Edgar Tekere") in smuggling themselves into Mozambique.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200223Meredith20024%E2%80%935-112) Mugabe remained in exile there for two years.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith20025-113) Mozambique's Marxist President [Samora Machel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samora_Machel "Samora Machel") was sceptical of Mugabe's leadership abilities and was unsure whether to recognise him as ZANU's legitimate leader. Machel gave him a house in [Quelimane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quelimane "Quelimane") and kept him under partial [house arrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_arrest "House arrest"), with Mugabe requiring permission to travel.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198180%E2%80%9381Blair200223-114) It would be almost a year before Machel accepted Mugabe's leadership of ZANU.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200223-109)

Mugabe travelled to various ZANLA camps in Mozambique to build support among its officers.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198181-115) By mid-1976, he had secured the allegiance of ZANLA's military commanders and established himself as the most prominent guerrilla leader battling Smith's regime.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200223-109) In August 1977, he was officially declared ZANU President at a meeting of the party's central committee held in [Chimoio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimoio "Chimoio").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson1981101Norman200862-116) During the war, Mugabe remained suspicious of many of ZANLA's commanders and had a number of them imprisoned.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200224-117) In 1977 he imprisoned his former second-in-command, [Wilfred Mhanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilfred_Mhanda?action=edit&redlink=1 "Wilfred Mhanda (page does not exist)"), for suspected disloyalty.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200224-117) After [Josiah Tongogara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josiah_Tongogara "Josiah Tongogara") was killed in a car accident in 1979, there were suggestions made that Mugabe may have had some involvement in it; these rumours were never substantiated.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200224Holland200855%E2%80%9356-118)

Mugabe remained aloof from the day-to-day military operations of ZANLA, which he entrusted to Tongogara.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200223-109) In January 1976, ZANLA launched its first major infiltration from Mozambique, with nearly 1000 guerrillas crossing the border to attack white-owned farms and stores.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198183Norman200860-119) In response, Smith's government enlisted all men under the age of 35, expanding the Rhodesian army by 50%.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198183Norman200860-119) ZANLA's attacks forced large numbers of white landowners to abandon their farms; their now-unemployed black workers joined ZANLA by the thousands.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson1981100-120) By 1979, ZANLA were in a position to attack a number of Rhodesian cities.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson1981115%E2%80%93116-121) Over the course of the war, at least 30,000 people were killed.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200210-122) As a proportion of their wider population, the whites had higher number of fatalities,[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200210-122) and by the latter part of the decade the guerrillas were winning.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson1981109-123)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Robert_Mugabe_%26_Nicolae_Ceau%C8%99escu%2C_Romania_1976.jpg/250px-Robert_Mugabe_%26_Nicolae_Ceau%C8%99escu%2C_Romania_1976.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robert_Mugabe_&_Nicolae_Ceau%C8%99escu,_Romania_1976.jpg)

Mugabe in a meeting with Romanian communist leader [Nicolae Ceaușescu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolae_Ceau%C8%99escu "Nicolae Ceaușescu") in 1976

Mugabe focused on the propaganda war, making regular speeches and radio broadcasts.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200223-109) In these, he presented himself as a [Marxist-Leninist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxist-Leninist "Marxist-Leninist"), speaking warmly of Marxist-Leninist revolutionaries like [Vladimir Lenin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Lenin "Vladimir Lenin"), [Joseph Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stalin "Joseph Stalin"), and [Fidel Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro "Fidel Castro").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200224-117) Despite his Marxist views, Mugabe's meetings with Soviet representatives were unproductive, for they insisted on Nkomo's leadership of the revolutionary struggle.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198188Norman200861-124) His relationship with the People's Republic of China was far warmer, as the Chinese Maoist government supplied ZANLA with armaments without any conditions.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198188-125) He also sought support from Western nations, visiting Western embassies in Mozambique,[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198189-126) and travelled to both Western states like Italy and Switzerland and Marxist-governed states like the Soviet Union, China, North Korea, Vietnam, and Cuba.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198199,_109,_114Norman200861,_63%E2%80%9364-127)

Mugabe called for the overthrow of Rhodesia's predominately white government, the execution of Smith and his "criminal gang", the expropriation of white-owned land, and the transformation of Rhodesia into a [one-party Marxist state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_state "Communist state").[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith20027-128) He repeatedly called for violence against the country's white minority,[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200211-129) referring to white Rhodesians as "blood-sucking exploiters", "sadistic killers", and "hard-core racists".[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200224-117) In one typical example, taken from a 1978 radio address, Mugabe declared: "Let us hammer [the white man] to defeat. Let us blow up his citadel. Let us give him no time to rest. Let us chase him in every corner. Let us rid our home of this settler vermin".[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200211-129) For Mugabe, armed struggle was an essential part of the establishment of a new state.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith20022-130) In contrast to other black nationalist leaders like Nkomo, Mugabe opposed a negotiated settlement with Smith's government.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith20022-130) In October 1976 ZANU nevertheless established a joint platform with ZAPU known as the Patriotic Front.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson198192%E2%80%9394Norman200861-131) In September 1978 Mugabe met with Nkomo in Lusaka. He was angry with the latter's secret attempts to negotiate with Smith.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson1981112-132)

### Lancaster House Agreement: 1979

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Mugabe&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Lancaster House Agreement: 1979")]

The beginning of the end for Smith came when South African Prime Minister [B. J. Vorster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._J._Vorster "B. J. Vorster") concluded that white minority rule was unsustainable in a country where blacks outnumbered whites 22:1.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-impression-133) Under pressure from Vorster, Smith accepted in principle that white minority rule could not be maintained forever. He oversaw the [1979 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_Zimbabwe_Rhodesia_general_election "1979 Zimbabwe Rhodesia general election") which resulted in [Abel Muzorewa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Muzorewa "Abel Muzorewa"), a politically moderate black bishop, being elected prime minister of the reconstituted [Zimbabwe Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Rhodesia "Zimbabwe Rhodesia"). Both ZANU and ZAPU had boycotted the election, which did not receive international recognition.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson1981117Norman200863-134) At the [Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting 1979](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Heads_of_Government_Meeting_1979 "Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting 1979"), held in Lusaka, the British prime minister [Margaret Thatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher "Margaret Thatcher") surprised delegates by announcing that the UK would officially recognise the country's independence if it transitioned to democratic majority rule.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson1981118%E2%80%93120-135)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Lancaster_House_%285880536589%29.jpg/250px-Lancaster_House_%285880536589%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lancaster_House_(5880536589).jpg)

Lancaster House in London's St James's district

The negotiations took place at [Lancaster House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House "Lancaster House") in London and were led by the [Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") politician [Peter Carington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Carington "Peter Carington").[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolland200858-136) Mugabe refused to attend these London peace talks,[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith20026%E2%80%937-137) opposing the idea of a negotiated rather than military solution to the Rhodesian War.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson1981122Holland200860-138) Machel insisted that he must, threatening to end Mozambican support for the ZANU-PF if he did not.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith20027Holland200860Norman200869Tendi2011310-139) Mugabe arrived in London in September 1979.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson1981122Meredith20027-140) There, he and Nkomo presented themselves as part of the "Patriotic Front" but established separate headquarters in the city.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200238Holland200858-141) At the conference the pair were divided in their attitude; Nkomo wanted to present himself as a moderate while Mugabe played up to his image as a Marxist revolutionary, with Carrington exploiting this division.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolland200861-142) Throughout the negotiations, Mugabe did not trust the British and believed that they were manipulating events to their own advantage.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson1981122%E2%80%93123Meredith20027%E2%80%938-143)

The ensuing [Lancaster House Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House_Agreement "Lancaster House Agreement") called for all participants in the Rhodesian Bush War to agree to a ceasefire, with a British governor, [Christopher Soames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Soames "Christopher Soames"), arriving in Rhodesia to oversee an election in which the various factions could compete as political parties.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith20028Norman200867-144) It outlined a plan for a transition to formal independence as a sovereign republic under black-majority rule, also maintaining that Rhodesia would be renamed Zimbabwe, a name adopted from the Iron Age archaeological site of [Great Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe "Great Zimbabwe").[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200211Norman200869-145) The agreement also ensured that the country's white minority retained many of its economic and political privileges,[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTETendi2011313-146) with 20 seats to be reserved for whites in the new Parliament.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithSimpson1981127Norman200867Tendi2011311-147) By insisting on the need for a democratic black majority government, Carington was able to convince Mugabe to compromise on the other main issue of the conference, that of land ownership.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolland200862%E2%80%9363-148) Mugabe agreed to the protection of the white community's privately owned property on the condition that the UK and U.S. governments provide financial assistance allowing the Zimbabwean government to purchase much land for redistribution among blacks.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolland200863-149) Mugabe was opposed to the idea of a ceasefire, but under pressure from Machel he agreed to it.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith20028-150) Mugabe signed the agreement, but felt cheated,[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith20028-150) remaining disappointed that he had never achieved a military victory over the Rhodesian forces.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith2002235Tendi2011313-151)

### Electoral campaign: 1980

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Mugabe&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Electoral campaign: 1980")]

Returning to Salisbury in January 1980, Mugabe was greeted by a supportive crowd.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith20029Norman200870-152) He settled into a house in [Mount Pleasant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Pleasant,_Harare "Mount Pleasant, Harare"), a wealthy, white-dominated suburb.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200213Norman200871-153) Machel had cautioned Mugabe not to alienate Rhodesia's white minority, warning him that any white flight after the election would cause economic damage as it had in Mozambique.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith20029Norman2008101Tendi2011313-154) Accordingly, during his electoral campaign, Mugabe avoided the use of Marxist and revolutionary rhetoric.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith20029-155) Mugabe insisted that in the election, ZANU would stand as a separate party to ZAPU, and refused Nkomo's request for a meeting.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200238Norman200870-156) He formed ZANU into a political party, known as [Zimbabwe African National Union – Patriotic Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Union_%E2%80%93_Patriotic_Front "Zimbabwe African National Union – Patriotic Front") (ZANU–PF).[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorman200870-157) Predictions were made that ZANU–PF would win the election on the basis of the country's ethnic divisions; Mugabe was Shona, a community that made up around 70% of the country's population, while Nkomo was Ndebele, a tribal group who made up only around 20%.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200212-158) For many in the white community and in the British government, this outcome was a terrifying prospect due to Mugabe's avowed Marxist beliefs and the inflammatory comments that he had made about whites during the guerrilla war.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200211-129)

During the campaign, Mugabe survived two assassination attempts.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200211Norman200871-159) In the first, which took place on 6 February, a grenade was thrown at his Mount Pleasant home, where it exploded against a garden wall.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200211Norman200871-159) In the second, on 10 February, [a roadside bomb exploded near his motorcade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_accidents_and_incidents_involving_Robert_Mugabe's_motorcade#List_of_accidents_and_incidents_resulting_in_injury_or_death "List of accidents and incidents involving Robert Mugabe's motorcade") as he left a [Fort Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masvingo "Masvingo") rally. Mugabe himself was unharmed.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200211Norman200871-159) Mugabe accused the Rhodesian security forces of being responsible for these attacks.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200211-160) In an attempt to quell the possibility that Rhodesia's security forces would launch a coup to prevent the election, Mugabe met with [Peter Walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Walls "Peter Walls"), the commander of Rhodesia's armed forces, and asked him to remain in his position in the event of a ZANU–PF victory. At the time Walls refused.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200212-161)

The electoral campaign was marred by widespread [voter intimidation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voter_intimidation "Voter intimidation"), perpetrated by Nkomo's ZAPU, [Abel Muzorewa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Muzorewa "Abel Muzorewa")'s [United African National Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_African_National_Council "United African National Council") (UANC), and Mugabe's ZANU–PF.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200210Norman200873-162) Commenting on ZANU–PF's activities in eastern Rhodesia, Nkomo complained that "the word _intimidation_ is mild. People are being terrorised. It is _terror_."[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200210-163) Reacting to ZANU–PF's acts of voter intimidation, Mugabe was called before Soames at Government House. Mugabe regarded the meeting as a British attempt to thwart his electoral campaign.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200210%E2%80%9311-164) Under the terms of the negotiation, Soames had the power to disqualify any political party guilty of voter intimidation.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200211-160) Rhodesia's security services, Nkomo, Muzorewa, and some of his own advisers all called on Soames to disqualify ZANU–PF. After deliberation, Soames disagreed, believing that ZANU–PF were sure to win the election and that disqualifying them would wreck any chance of an [orderly transition of power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orderly_transition_of_power "Orderly transition of power").[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200211-160)

In [the February election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Southern_Rhodesian_general_election "1980 Southern Rhodesian general election"), ZANU–PF secured 63% of the national vote, gaining 57 of the 80 parliamentary seats allocated for black parties and providing them with an [absolute majority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_of_the_entire_membership "Majority of the entire membership").[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200212Meredith200213Norman200873-165) ZAPU had gained 20 seats, and UANC had three.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair200212-158) Mugabe was elected MP for the Salisbury constituency of [Highfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highfield_(parliamentary_constituency)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Highfield (parliamentary constituency) (page does not exist)").[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlair2002156-166) Attempting to calm panic and prevent white flight, Mugabe appeared on television and called for national unity, stability, and law and order, insisting that the pensions of white civil servants would be guaranteed and that private property would be protected.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200213Holland2008xiiiNorman200874-167)

## Premiership (1980–1987)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Mugabe&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Premiership (1980–1987)")]

Statues atop the tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Heroes' Acre; the monument was designed by North Korean architects who reported directly to Mugabe.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolland2008194-168)

Mugabe's government continued to make regular pronouncements about converting Zimbabwe into a socialist society.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200278-185) In contrast to Mugabe's talk of socialism, his government's budgetary policies were conservative, operating within a capitalist framework and emphasising the need for foreign investment.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith200248-177) In office, Mugabe From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Zambian politician (born 1976)

**Moses F Moyo** (born 16 August 1976) is a Zambian politician. He is a Member of Parliament and also the 2nd Deputy Speaker of The [National Assembly of Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_Zambia "National Assembly of Zambia") since 3 September 2021.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Moyo#cite_note-1)

Moyo is independent and represents [Luangeni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luangeni "Luangeni") constituency.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Moyo#cite_note-2)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Zambian politician (born 1976)

**Moses F Moyo** (born 16 August 1976) is a Zambian politician. He is a Member of Parliament and also the 2nd Deputy Speaker of The [National Assembly of Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_Zambia "National Assembly of Zambia") since 3 September 2021.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Moyo#cite_note-1)

Moyo is independent and represents [Luangeni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luangeni "Luangeni") constituency.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Moyo#cite_note-2)
