**City Harvest Church** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"):城市丰收教会) or **CHC** is a [pentecostal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecostal "Pentecostal")[megachurch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megachurch "Megachurch") in [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore").

Founded in 1989 by Kong Hee,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-news.asiaone.com-1) the church officially bases its values on [Charismatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charismatic_movement "Charismatic movement") and [Pentecostal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecostalism "Pentecostalism") teachings, with emphases on such doctrines as [the Great Commandment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Commandment "Great Commandment"), [the Great Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Commission "Great Commission") and [the Cultural Mandate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_mandate "Cultural mandate").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-TheCityHarvestStory-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-sof-3)

City Harvest Church is a congregational member of the [National Council of Churches of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Council_of_Churches_of_Singapore "National Council of Churches of Singapore").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-4) Services are held at its church building in Jurong West and rented hall space at [Suntec International Convention Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suntec_City#Suntec_Singapore_International_Convention_and_Exhibition_Centre "Suntec City").

In 2015, six church leaders and fund or finance managers were found guilty of criminal [breach of trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breach_of_fiduciary_duties "Breach of fiduciary duties") and falsification of accounts. When all six of them appealed against the verdict and sentences, the Appeal Court found them guilty of basic criminal breach of trust and reduced their sentences. The Court also noted that the six were not motivated by personal gain, and no permanent loss was intended or caused to CHC – all the monies were returned to the church with interest.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-JudgmentMagistrateAppeals-8)

The church was one of three megachurches to make it to a list of Singapore's 10 largest charities, according to a report by _[The Straits Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Straits\_Times "The Straits Times")_ in 2019.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-9)

## Overview

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=City_Harvest_Church&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Overview")]

CHC has two main worship venues:[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-Chong2018-10) its conventional church, completed in 2002 in the western part of the island, which emphasizes size and modern aesthetics and has a main hall capacity of 2,300 people; and the downtown Suntec Singapore Convention & Exhibition Centre, used since 2010 for its larger worship space.

The church's building features four levels of basement. It has been cited by Singapore Records as the "world's deepest church."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-11) With a main auditorium spanning 1,700 square meters, the church is also listed by Singapore Records as the largest church structure in the South-East Asian Peninsula.

_[The Straits Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Straits\_Times "The Straits Times")_ reported that CHC's congregation size peaked at 33,000 in 2010 before investigations into its leaders began.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-ST_25yrs-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-City_Harvest_sees_fewer_followers_but_remains_among_top_10_richest_charities-13) In 2012, [Global Church Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Church_Network "Global Church Network") listed CHC as one of the ten largest churches outside of the US.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-10_Global_Churches_Larger_than_America%E2%80%99s_Largest-14) The church reported that it had a congregation size of 15,654 in 2019 and an average weekly viewership of 17,276 for its online services and resources in 2020.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-City_Harvest_Annual_Report_2019_/_2020-15) CHC exhibits a young membership profile relative to established mainline denominations. As of 2014, 13.9% of the membership are between 20 and 24 years old, and 49.2% are between the ages of 25 and 45. As of 2018, the demographics revealed that 45.1% are men, 54.9% are women, 34.1% are married, and 61.9% are single. 55.9% of them are working adults, while most of the rest are serving the military, non-salaried, students, or children.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-City_Harvest_Annual_Report_2018-16) As of 2025, the church reported a congregation size of 24,546. The cumulative membership, including its 269 branch and affiliate churches stands at 80,040.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-17)

The church was founded by Kong Hee[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-news.asiaone.com-1)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-BioKongHee-18) and his wife [Sun Ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ho_Yeow_Sun "Ho Yeow Sun")[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-broadpastor-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-BioSunHo-20) on 7 May 1989 and held its first service at Peace Centre. It first functioned as "Ekklesia Ministry," a youth department under the legal covering of Bethany Christian Centre, an [Assemblies of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assemblies_of_God "Assemblies of God") church. On 21 December 1992, City Harvest Church was set up as a society. It was registered as a charity with the Singapore government on 16 October 1993.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-21)

From 2002, Kong began to teach on the [Cultural Mandate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Mandate "Cultural Mandate") and encourage the church members to excel in the marketplace. On 1 November 2005, Kong withdrew himself from the staff payroll and he now serves the church as an honorary founder/senior pastor.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-CHCStory-22) Later, in an investigation leading to trial and conviction, it was revealed that Kong had set up a private fund and diverted over $3 million of tithes and pledges to a 'multi purpose account'. Givers to the account were told this was for the funding of a 'Crossover project'.

CHC founded the City Harvest Community Services Association (CHCSA) in 1997.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-KongHeeDenyUsingSham-23)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-BioSunHo-20) CHCSA is involved in elderly services, direct social services, patient care services, as well as youth and community projects.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-24) In December 2004, CHC was involved in the humanitarian relief work of the [Indian Ocean tsunami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Indian_Ocean_earthquake_and_tsunami "2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-ST_25yrs-12) The church sent aid and disaster relief workers to the [2010 Haiti earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Haiti_earthquake "2010 Haiti earthquake").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-25)

CHC has actively pursued [church planting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_planting "Church planting") and evangelism across the region.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-Chong2018-10)

## Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=City_Harvest_Church&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Controversies")]

### Criminal Breach of Trust

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=City_Harvest_Church&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Criminal Breach of Trust")]

Main article: [City Harvest Church Criminal Breach of Trust Case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church_Criminal_Breach_of_Trust_Case "City Harvest Church Criminal Breach of Trust Case")

Since the beginning of the 21st century, one of the biggest corruption case on the island[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-27) revolved around City Harvest Church and founders Kong Hee involving a total of S$50 million of funds misused. Six persons from the senior leadership, including its church founder Kong Hee, were convicted of the misuse of millions of dollars of the church's money.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-city_harvest-28) The court found that the church's senior leadership had channeled $24 million from CHC's Building Fund into sham bonds in music production company Xtron and glass-maker Firna.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-city_harvest-28) The purpose of the restricted Building Fund was specifically for building or investment.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-29) They used the money to fund the singing career of Kong's wife [Ho Yeow Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ho_Yeow_Sun "Ho Yeow Sun"), as part of the Crossover Project, a church mission which they said was to evangelise through Ms Ho's music.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-city_harvest-28) Expenses revealed by court records included a house in [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los Angeles") that cost $28,000 a month in rent; a whole entourage of staff; a $1.9 million paycheck to rapper [Wyclef Jean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyclef_Jean "Wyclef Jean") to produce the "China Wine" video; as well as another $500,000 to sweep up her albums when they tanked.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-30)

The six appealed the verdict, and on 7 April 2017, the [Court of Appeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore_Court_of_Appeal "Singapore Court of Appeal") reduced their sentences by approximately half, based on its finding that “the appellants should only have been convicted of the offence of criminal breach of trust simpliciter under section 406 of the Penal Code”. The judges said it was a situation that involved no personal gain on the part of the six, and that they believed their acts, especially in sham investments would advance the interest of the church.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-city_harvest-28)

A Criminal Reference filed by the AGC in a bid to reinstate the original convictions was heard by a five-judge Court of Appeal and dismissed on 1 Feb 2018.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-31)

### "Words of comfort" Sermon

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=City_Harvest_Church&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: \"Words of comfort\" Sermon")]

In 2012, during a sermon delivered by Kong which was recorded and later posted on [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube"), Kong said that he identified with the experience of Jesus Christ at his crucifixion and that God said in reply "I'm so sorry, but you need to go through this by yourself, to bring a change to your generation.".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-:0-32) While viewers of the video interpreted that Kong said that God apologized to Kong for the church's legal troubles and drew overwhelming negative responses.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-:0-32) In response, _[The Christian Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Christian\_Post "The Christian Post")_ said that it was taken out of context and interpreted wrongly and that it should be treated as words of comfort for Kong's ensuing trial.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-:1-33) Some City Harvest Church worshippers responded in kind that it should be interpreted as words of comfort.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-:0-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-:1-33)

### Sun Ho Hacking Incident

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=City_Harvest_Church&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Sun Ho Hacking Incident")]

In 2013, a hacking incident took place involving founding clergy Sun Ho after hackers self-styled "Messiah" hacked her official website,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-35) following which a police report was made by City Harvest Church.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-36) Around the same time, a spam-like email was further published on the Internet that involved another self-styled "Messiah-Two" making allegations regarding her.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-37) The suspected "Messiah", James Raj, [was arrested](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Singapore_cyberattacks "2013 Singapore cyberattacks") the same year for hacking into the website of the [Prime Minister's Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister's_Office_(Singapore) "Prime Minister's Office (Singapore)"). He had prior drug convictions.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-38)

### S$310 million Suntec investment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=City_Harvest_Church&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: S$310 million Suntec investment")]

On 6 March 2010, City Harvest Church announced that it had purchased a significant stake in [Suntec Convention Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suntec_Convention_Centre "Suntec Convention Centre") and will be using its facilities for church services, the project will cost an estimated S$310 million, including shares acquisition, renovation, and rental costs.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-asiaone-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-todayonline_building-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-CNA-building-41) Church founder Kong Hee said in a statement that the move "allows [the church] to move from a present expensive rental model to a more financially sustainable ownership model for the long term".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-42) However, some brought up the point that as a registered charity, CHC's income – expected to include profits and dividends from space rental and tenant leases in Suntec Singapore in the future – is non-taxable. The church has clarified that the investment is indirect, through a wholly owned subsidiary for the purpose of taxation and separate accounting. Questions surfaced among the public whether religious organizations, which are registered as charities, should be allowed to go into business using what are essentially donor funds.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-asiaone-39)

The [Commissioner of Charities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioner_of_Charities?action=edit&redlink=1 "Commissioner of Charities (page does not exist)") (COC) sought clarifications on the transaction.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-todayonline_building-40) The church stated it was under a [non-disclosure agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-disclosure_agreement "Non-disclosure agreement") which required the details of the transaction to remain confidential, but explained that the investment was made through a holding company that is not a charity organization and does not enjoy tax breaks; and had disclosed details of the deal to the COC as well as the [Urban Redevelopment Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_Redevelopment_Authority "Urban Redevelopment Authority") upon request.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-43) The church also said that there was a "strong and unfounded allegation" floating online that the management board and Kong were "deliberately concealing a number of embarrassing facts from its members" with regard to the Suntec investment, saying that the allegation was "furthest from the truth",[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-CNA-building-41) and later released a notice stating that Charities and foundations often use donor funds to invest and generate sustainable income for their intended causes.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-44)

On 21 July 2012, the church announced details of its investment in Suntec Singapore. A total of 39.2% shareholding was acquired at a total cost of $97.75 million. Public-listed Suntec REIT holds the other 60.8%. The remaining balance in the projected building fund will be used for costs such as equipment, furniture and fittings, periodical shifting costs (due to other events at the venue), committed rentals, optional rentals and refundable rental deposits.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church#cite_note-46) In 2013, it was revealed that the church had undertaken a $50m loan with high interest to finance the acquisition of additional shares, as the building fund had largely been exhausted over the years on venue and equipment rentals, while using the Singapore Expo from 2006 to 2010. If the church is unable to finance the loan, it may in default lose up to 19.2% of its shareholding as part of the loan agreement.

**Kong Hee** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"):康希; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"):_Kāng Xī_; born 23 August 1964) is the founder and senior pastor of City Harvest Church.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-BioKongHee-2)

He was convicted in 2015 of being involved in the [City Harvest Church Criminal Breach of Trust Case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church_Criminal_Breach_of_Trust_Case "City Harvest Church Criminal Breach of Trust Case"), Singapore's biggest case in misuse of charitable funds.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-3)[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-4)[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-5) He was seen to be the "key man" behind the scandal[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-6) who had guided his five accomplices by the Singapore court of three charges of criminal breach of trust.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-guilty-7) Although Kong and the five were guilty of serious breaches, the court noted that the $50 million was also ultimately returned to the church.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-defence-nowrongfulgain-8)

He served his sentence at Changi Prison Complex from 21 April 2017 to 22 August 2019.[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-9)[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-needtoknow-10)

Kong is also involved in the Christian [Charismatic Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charismatic_Movement "Charismatic Movement"), a philosophy of ministry that emphasises the [Great Commandment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Commandment "Great Commandment"), the [Great Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Commission "Great Commission") and the [Cultural Mandate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Mandate "Cultural Mandate").[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-11)

## Early life

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Kong is the fifth child of Kong Leng, a [professional engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_engineer "Professional engineer"), and Toh Poh-Eng, a diamond trader. From 1975 to 1988, Kong was a member of [Marine Parade Christian Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Parade_Christian_Centre?action=edit&redlink=1 "Marine Parade Christian Centre (page does not exist)"), an [Anglican church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_church "Anglican church") located in eastern Singapore. He studied at [Raffles Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raffles_Institution "Raffles Institution") (1977–1981), [Raffles Junior College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raffles_Junior_College "Raffles Junior College") (1982) as well as [National University of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_University_of_Singapore "National University of Singapore"), [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") (Computer & Information Sciences) (1985–1988).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

During his university years, he worked part-time for the [Chapel of the Resurrection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_the_Resurrection "Chapel of the Resurrection") under the oversight of Anglican vicar, Reverend Dr. [Canon James Wong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canon_James_Wong?action=edit&redlink=1 "Canon James Wong (page does not exist)"). During that tenure, he helped Canon Wong set up a new congregation, [Orchard Christian Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchard_Christian_Centre?action=edit&redlink=1 "Orchard Christian Centre (page does not exist)"). Upon university graduation in 1988, Kong worked a short stint in a local publishing house as a programmer.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1989, Kong was a staff evangelist with "[Christ For Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_For_Asia?action=edit&redlink=1 "Christ For Asia (page does not exist)")", a missions organisation in the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines") led by [Assemblies of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assemblies_of_God "Assemblies of God") minister, Reverend [Randy Sing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Sing?action=edit&redlink=1 "Randy Sing (page does not exist)"). At that same time, there was an opportunity for Kong to pioneer a new church in Singapore. With the support and encouragement of some senior pastors in the city, Kong decided to relocate back to Singapore and helped set up a new congregation with 20 youths.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-BioKongHee-2)

## City Harvest Church

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: City Harvest Church")]

Main article: City Harvest Church

On 7 May 1989, City Harvest Church was founded as a department (known as "Ekklesia Ministry") of Bethany Christian Centre (Assemblies of God).[[12]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-12)

From 1997, Kong was the executive director of the [Festival of Praise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_of_Praise "Festival of Praise"), an annual event that brought together churches for united prayer and worship.[_[needs update?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] Kong was a board member of Dr. [David Yonggi Cho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Yonggi_Cho "David Yonggi Cho")'s [Church Growth International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Growth_International?action=edit&redlink=1 "Church Growth International (page does not exist)") (South Korea) and Dr. [Luis Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Bush "Luis Bush")'s Transform World (Indonesia). Kong is a protege,[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-13) friend and mentee[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-14) of [Phil Pringle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Pringle "Phil Pringle"), the founder and senior pastor of [C3 Church Global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C3_Church_Global "C3 Church Global") (Australia) and advisory pastor to City Harvest Church.[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-15) With his wife [Sun Ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ho "Sun Ho"), they once owned two companies, [International Harvest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Harvest?action=edit&redlink=1 "International Harvest (page does not exist)") and [Skin Couture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skin_Couture?action=edit&redlink=1 "Skin Couture (page does not exist)").

In December 2010, City Harvest Church had an average of 23,256 attendees[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-CHCStory-16) with 47 affiliate "Harvest" churches, as well as 29 affiliate churches and 6 Bible schools in Asia, namely, in Singapore, Australia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Taiwan. Another 18 affiliate churches in East and West Malaysia are under the [Malaysian Harvest Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysian_Harvest_Fellowship?action=edit&redlink=1 "Malaysian Harvest Fellowship (page does not exist)") which Kong Hee co-founded.[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-17)[[18]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-18)[[19]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-19)[[20]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-20)

## Conviction

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Conviction")]

Main article: [City Harvest Church Criminal Breach of Trust Case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church_Criminal_Breach_of_Trust_Case "City Harvest Church Criminal Breach of Trust Case")

### Investigations

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Investigations")]

On 31 May 2010, the Office of the Commissioner of Charities and the [Commercial Affairs Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Affairs_Department "Commercial Affairs Department") of the Singapore Police began investigating more than 16 individuals linked to City Harvest Church, including church founder Kong Hee and his wife, [Sun Ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ho "Sun Ho").[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-21)[[22]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-22) The police were looking into financial transactions involving the possible falsification of accounts and criminal breach of trust amounting to millions of dollars which dated back a number of years. The authorities allowed regular church activities and services to continue for the congregation during ongoing investigations.[[23]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-23)[[24]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-24)[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-25)[[26]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-26)[[27]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-27)

On 26 June 2012, the Commissioner of Charities released a press statement detailing the results of its inquiry. It stated that there were misconduct and mismanagement in the administration of City Harvest Church. There were irregularities of at least $23 million in the church's funds, which were used to finance [Sun Ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ho_Yeow_Sun "Ho Yeow Sun")'s secular music career. There was also a concerted effort to conceal this movement of funds from stakeholders. Kong Hee and seven others were suspended from their roles in the church.[[28]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-28)

A subsequent report indicated that the investigations were trigged by complaints made to the authorities.[[29]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-29)

### Arrests and charges

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Arrests and charges")]

Also on 26 June 2012, Kong Hee and four other leaders of City Harvest Church were arrested and charged with misuse of funds.[[30]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-30)[[31]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-31) A sixth leader was charged on 25 July 2012. All six accused were granted bail of S$500,000 and had their passports impounded.[[32]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-32)

### Trial and conviction

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Trial and conviction")]

The trial of Kong Hee and the five other leaders commenced in May 2013 and was adjourned several times.[[33]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-33)[[34]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-34)[[35]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-35) There was a total of 142 days of hearings.[[36]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-36)

The verdicts were announced on 21 October 2015. Kong Hee and the other five leaders were found guilty of all charges.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-guilty-7)

Sentencing was on 20 November 2015. Kong Hee received the heaviest sentence of the six, 8 years in prison.[[37]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-37)[[38]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-38) Following a request from the defendants, the judge agreed to defer the start of the sentences until 11 January 2016.[[39]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-39)[[40]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-40)

### Related decisions

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Related decisions")]

In 2017, the Commissioner of Charities permanently barred the six in the case, with two additional church executive members, [Kelvin Teo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin_Teo "Kelvin Teo") Meng How and Tan Su Pheng Jacqueline, from holding key management positions or being a board member in City Harvest Church or any other charity. Additionally the church was barred from paying the legal fees for the six. However, they were still allowed to perform their religious activities.[[41]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-41)

### Appeals

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Appeals")]

On 27 November 2015, it was reported that the Attorney General's Chambers had filed appeals against the sentence issued to Kong Hee and the five other defendants, on the grounds that it was "manifestly inadequate".[[42]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-42)

On 2 December 2015, it was reported that Kong Hee and the other five defendants had also filed appeals.[[43]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-43)

On 4 March 2016, it was reported that the appeal hearing would commence on 19 September 2016.[[44]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-44)

On 7 April 2017, his original sentence of 8 years in prison was reduced to 3.5 years.[[45]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-45) In delivering their decision, the judges noted that there was no element of wrongful gain or personal financial benefit, either direct or indirect.[[46]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-defence-nowrongfulgain2-46)[[47]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-47)[[48]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-48) The Court of Appeal acknowledged that “The theological legitimacy of the Crossover as a means of evangelism is not an issue in this case.” (Para 1)[[49]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-Inquiry-Misconduct-49) “The Crossover – which is central to the entire case – is an evangelistic endeavour to spread the gospel through the secular music of Sun Ho. It is not disputed that the Crossover had the full support of the CHC Board.” (Para 21)[[49]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-Inquiry-Misconduct-49)

Pages 264-267 of the appeal judgement characterised Kong as "coloured by greed and self-interest", as the Crossover project appeared to have been designed to benefit Sun Ho and Kong Hee. Sun Ho's contract with Xtron (a company controlled by Kong Hee) was to entitle Sun to 25% of gross income (estimated to reach US$30M[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]) regardless of project costs, in addition to a monthly salary of US$10,000.[[50]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-50) However, this contract between Sun Ho and Xtron was terminated in August 2008.[[51]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-51)

In addition, he had told members they were off-salary from the church. A private fund was set up to and raised over $3 million “to fund the [Crossover] Project” and was fully expended in just 3 years for the purposes of the Project.[[49]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-Inquiry-Misconduct-49)

Kong Hee began serving his sentence on 21 April 2017.

### Comments by the Minister for Law

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Comments by the Minister for Law")]

| External videos |
| --- |
| [![Image 5: video icon](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg/20px-Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg)[Law minister K Shanmugam setting out the government's position on the court's ruling](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QDiuG2HTHOo), Gov.sg video |

Expressing his disappointment by the Court of Appeal's decision to overrule a 1976 High Court decision, which had held that company directors could be convicted for criminal breach of trust under section 409 of the Penal Code, [Minister for Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_for_Law "Minister for Law")[K Shanmugam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K_Shanmugam "K Shanmugam") said, “The government believes the sentences are too low. But the sentences reflect the law as it stands after the High Court’s decision last year confirmed by the Court of Appeal. The courts decide these matters. All of us have to respect the decision regardless of whether we agree or disagree with it.”

“It is now up to Parliament to amend the law, and that we should do soon. We will ensure that legislation provides for higher penalties for directors and other senior officers who commit criminal breach of trust,” he added.[[52]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-52)

### Release

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Release")]

On 22 August 2019, Kong Hee was released from prison, having served 2 years and 4 months of the sentence.[[53]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-53) Inmates typically serve two-thirds of their sentence before released on remission for good behaviour.[[54]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-54)

In his first appearance at the church after his release, Kong delivered a four-minute speech apologising to church members for "any pain, anxiety, disappointment, or grief that you have suffered because of me".[[55]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-55)

## Controversies

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Controversies")]

### Plagiarism

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Plagiarism")]

In March 2010, a blogger identified plagiarism on Kong Hee's _Daily Devotionals_ as they were similar to writings in another publication, _[The Leadership Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Leadership\_Bible?action=edit&redlink=1 "The Leadership Bible (page does not exist)")_ which had been published ten years prior. The copied text were published as physical copies into two books, _[Renewing Your Spiritual Energy in 90 Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renewing\_Your\_Spiritual\_Energy\_in\_90\_Days?action=edit&redlink=1 "Renewing Your Spiritual Energy in 90 Days (page does not exist)")_, without accreditation to the original authors. Kong Hee's daily devotionals were originally compiled from his personal reading notes and printed as supplementary reading for his members, free of charge. Some years later, due to popular demand overseas, a local publisher compiled and released foreign language translations of the devotional for sale.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Kong Hee posted a note on his website and explained that the devotion was "originally meant only for internal circulation among the members of my church. As such, there was an oversight in not quoting the sources of some portions that borrow from the writings of other Christian authors." There was also an apology for the oversight.[[56]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-56)[[57]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-ST-plagiarisedBook-57)

The publisher, who is also a member of City Harvest Church, acknowledged that at the time of publication, both himself and Mr Kong were aware that certain portions of the content were not original.[[57]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-ST-plagiarisedBook-57)[[58]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-58) The publisher of "Renewal" has since made amendments to the soft copies to include accreditation.

## Personal life

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Kong is married to pastor-turned-pop-singer [Ho Yeow Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ho_Yeow_Sun "Ho Yeow Sun"), also known as Sun Ho. They have one son, Dayan Kong, who was born in 2005.[[59]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-59)

Kong was the co-owner of a 5,242 sq ft duplex penthouse located on the 11th floor of The Oceanfront in the premium residential enclave [Sentosa Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentosa_Cove "Sentosa Cove"). The penthouse was co-owned with Indonesian tycoon Mr Wahju Hanafi, a church follower. The pair bought the penthouse for $9.33 million in 2007, each paying monthly installments of $17,000, before the apartment was sold at a loss of over S$2 million to a Kenyan diplomat.[[60]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-60)

**Kong Hee** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"):康希; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"):_Kāng Xī_; born 23 August 1964) is the founder and senior pastor of City Harvest Church.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-BioKongHee-2)

He was convicted in 2015 of being involved in the [City Harvest Church Criminal Breach of Trust Case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church_Criminal_Breach_of_Trust_Case "City Harvest Church Criminal Breach of Trust Case"), Singapore's biggest case in misuse of charitable funds.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-3)[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-4)[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-5) He was seen to be the "key man" behind the scandal[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-6) who had guided his five accomplices by the Singapore court of three charges of criminal breach of trust.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-guilty-7) Although Kong and the five were guilty of serious breaches, the court noted that the $50 million was also ultimately returned to the church.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-defence-nowrongfulgain-8)

He served his sentence at Changi Prison Complex from 21 April 2017 to 22 August 2019.[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-9)[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-needtoknow-10)

Kong is also involved in the Christian [Charismatic Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charismatic_Movement "Charismatic Movement"), a philosophy of ministry that emphasises the [Great Commandment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Commandment "Great Commandment"), the [Great Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Commission "Great Commission") and the [Cultural Mandate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Mandate "Cultural Mandate").[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-11)

## Early life

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Kong is the fifth child of Kong Leng, a [professional engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_engineer "Professional engineer"), and Toh Poh-Eng, a diamond trader. From 1975 to 1988, Kong was a member of [Marine Parade Christian Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Parade_Christian_Centre?action=edit&redlink=1 "Marine Parade Christian Centre (page does not exist)"), an [Anglican church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_church "Anglican church") located in eastern Singapore. He studied at [Raffles Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raffles_Institution "Raffles Institution") (1977–1981), [Raffles Junior College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raffles_Junior_College "Raffles Junior College") (1982) as well as [National University of Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_University_of_Singapore "National University of Singapore"), [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") (Computer & Information Sciences) (1985–1988).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

During his university years, he worked part-time for the [Chapel of the Resurrection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_the_Resurrection "Chapel of the Resurrection") under the oversight of Anglican vicar, Reverend Dr. [Canon James Wong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canon_James_Wong?action=edit&redlink=1 "Canon James Wong (page does not exist)"). During that tenure, he helped Canon Wong set up a new congregation, [Orchard Christian Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchard_Christian_Centre?action=edit&redlink=1 "Orchard Christian Centre (page does not exist)"). Upon university graduation in 1988, Kong worked a short stint in a local publishing house as a programmer.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1989, Kong was a staff evangelist with "[Christ For Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_For_Asia?action=edit&redlink=1 "Christ For Asia (page does not exist)")", a missions organisation in the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines") led by [Assemblies of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assemblies_of_God "Assemblies of God") minister, Reverend [Randy Sing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Sing?action=edit&redlink=1 "Randy Sing (page does not exist)"). At that same time, there was an opportunity for Kong to pioneer a new church in Singapore. With the support and encouragement of some senior pastors in the city, Kong decided to relocate back to Singapore and helped set up a new congregation with 20 youths.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-BioKongHee-2)

## City Harvest Church

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: City Harvest Church")]

Main article: City Harvest Church

On 7 May 1989, City Harvest Church was founded as a department (known as "Ekklesia Ministry") of Bethany Christian Centre (Assemblies of God).[[12]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-12)

From 1997, Kong was the executive director of the [Festival of Praise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_of_Praise "Festival of Praise"), an annual event that brought together churches for united prayer and worship.[_[needs update?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] Kong was a board member of Dr. [David Yonggi Cho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Yonggi_Cho "David Yonggi Cho")'s [Church Growth International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Growth_International?action=edit&redlink=1 "Church Growth International (page does not exist)") (South Korea) and Dr. [Luis Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Bush "Luis Bush")'s Transform World (Indonesia). Kong is a protege,[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-13) friend and mentee[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-14) of [Phil Pringle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Pringle "Phil Pringle"), the founder and senior pastor of [C3 Church Global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C3_Church_Global "C3 Church Global") (Australia) and advisory pastor to City Harvest Church.[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-15) With his wife [Sun Ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ho "Sun Ho"), they once owned two companies, [International Harvest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Harvest?action=edit&redlink=1 "International Harvest (page does not exist)") and [Skin Couture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skin_Couture?action=edit&redlink=1 "Skin Couture (page does not exist)").

In December 2010, City Harvest Church had an average of 23,256 attendees[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-CHCStory-16) with 47 affiliate "Harvest" churches, as well as 29 affiliate churches and 6 Bible schools in Asia, namely, in Singapore, Australia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Taiwan. Another 18 affiliate churches in East and West Malaysia are under the [Malaysian Harvest Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysian_Harvest_Fellowship?action=edit&redlink=1 "Malaysian Harvest Fellowship (page does not exist)") which Kong Hee co-founded.[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-17)[[18]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-18)[[19]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-19)[[20]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-20)

## Conviction

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Conviction")]

Main article: [City Harvest Church Criminal Breach of Trust Case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Harvest_Church_Criminal_Breach_of_Trust_Case "City Harvest Church Criminal Breach of Trust Case")

### Investigations

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Investigations")]

On 31 May 2010, the Office of the Commissioner of Charities and the [Commercial Affairs Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Affairs_Department "Commercial Affairs Department") of the Singapore Police began investigating more than 16 individuals linked to City Harvest Church, including church founder Kong Hee and his wife, [Sun Ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ho "Sun Ho").[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-21)[[22]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-22) The police were looking into financial transactions involving the possible falsification of accounts and criminal breach of trust amounting to millions of dollars which dated back a number of years. The authorities allowed regular church activities and services to continue for the congregation during ongoing investigations.[[23]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-23)[[24]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-24)[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-25)[[26]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-26)[[27]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-27)

On 26 June 2012, the Commissioner of Charities released a press statement detailing the results of its inquiry. It stated that there were misconduct and mismanagement in the administration of City Harvest Church. There were irregularities of at least $23 million in the church's funds, which were used to finance [Sun Ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ho_Yeow_Sun "Ho Yeow Sun")'s secular music career. There was also a concerted effort to conceal this movement of funds from stakeholders. Kong Hee and seven others were suspended from their roles in the church.[[28]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-28)

A subsequent report indicated that the investigations were trigged by complaints made to the authorities.[[29]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-29)

### Arrests and charges

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Arrests and charges")]

Also on 26 June 2012, Kong Hee and four other leaders of City Harvest Church were arrested and charged with misuse of funds.[[30]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-30)[[31]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-31) A sixth leader was charged on 25 July 2012. All six accused were granted bail of S$500,000 and had their passports impounded.[[32]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-32)

### Trial and conviction

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Trial and conviction")]

The trial of Kong Hee and the five other leaders commenced in May 2013 and was adjourned several times.[[33]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-33)[[34]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-34)[[35]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-35) There was a total of 142 days of hearings.[[36]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-36)

The verdicts were announced on 21 October 2015. Kong Hee and the other five leaders were found guilty of all charges.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-guilty-7)

Sentencing was on 20 November 2015. Kong Hee received the heaviest sentence of the six, 8 years in prison.[[37]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-37)[[38]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-38) Following a request from the defendants, the judge agreed to defer the start of the sentences until 11 January 2016.[[39]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-39)[[40]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-40)

### Related decisions

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Related decisions")]

In 2017, the Commissioner of Charities permanently barred the six in the case, with two additional church executive members, [Kelvin Teo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin_Teo "Kelvin Teo") Meng How and Tan Su Pheng Jacqueline, from holding key management positions or being a board member in City Harvest Church or any other charity. Additionally the church was barred from paying the legal fees for the six. However, they were still allowed to perform their religious activities.[[41]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-41)

### Appeals

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Appeals")]

On 27 November 2015, it was reported that the Attorney General's Chambers had filed appeals against the sentence issued to Kong Hee and the five other defendants, on the grounds that it was "manifestly inadequate".[[42]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-42)

On 2 December 2015, it was reported that Kong Hee and the other five defendants had also filed appeals.[[43]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-43)

On 4 March 2016, it was reported that the appeal hearing would commence on 19 September 2016.[[44]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-44)

On 7 April 2017, his original sentence of 8 years in prison was reduced to 3.5 years.[[45]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-45) In delivering their decision, the judges noted that there was no element of wrongful gain or personal financial benefit, either direct or indirect.[[46]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-defence-nowrongfulgain2-46)[[47]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-47)[[48]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-48) The Court of Appeal acknowledged that “The theological legitimacy of the Crossover as a means of evangelism is not an issue in this case.” (Para 1)[[49]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-Inquiry-Misconduct-49) “The Crossover – which is central to the entire case – is an evangelistic endeavour to spread the gospel through the secular music of Sun Ho. It is not disputed that the Crossover had the full support of the CHC Board.” (Para 21)[[49]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-Inquiry-Misconduct-49)

Pages 264-267 of the appeal judgement characterised Kong as "coloured by greed and self-interest", as the Crossover project appeared to have been designed to benefit Sun Ho and Kong Hee. Sun Ho's contract with Xtron (a company controlled by Kong Hee) was to entitle Sun to 25% of gross income (estimated to reach US$30M[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]) regardless of project costs, in addition to a monthly salary of US$10,000.[[50]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-50) However, this contract between Sun Ho and Xtron was terminated in August 2008.[[51]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-51)

In addition, he had told members they were off-salary from the church. A private fund was set up to and raised over $3 million “to fund the [Crossover] Project” and was fully expended in just 3 years for the purposes of the Project.[[49]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-Inquiry-Misconduct-49)

Kong Hee began serving his sentence on 21 April 2017.

### Comments by the Minister for Law

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Comments by the Minister for Law")]

| External videos |
| --- |
| [![Image 5: video icon](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg/20px-Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg)[Law minister K Shanmugam setting out the government's position on the court's ruling](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QDiuG2HTHOo), Gov.sg video |

Expressing his disappointment by the Court of Appeal's decision to overrule a 1976 High Court decision, which had held that company directors could be convicted for criminal breach of trust under section 409 of the Penal Code, [Minister for Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_for_Law "Minister for Law")[K Shanmugam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K_Shanmugam "K Shanmugam") said, “The government believes the sentences are too low. But the sentences reflect the law as it stands after the High Court’s decision last year confirmed by the Court of Appeal. The courts decide these matters. All of us have to respect the decision regardless of whether we agree or disagree with it.”

“It is now up to Parliament to amend the law, and that we should do soon. We will ensure that legislation provides for higher penalties for directors and other senior officers who commit criminal breach of trust,” he added.[[52]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-52)

### Release

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Release")]

On 22 August 2019, Kong Hee was released from prison, having served 2 years and 4 months of the sentence.[[53]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-53) Inmates typically serve two-thirds of their sentence before released on remission for good behaviour.[[54]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-54)

In his first appearance at the church after his release, Kong delivered a four-minute speech apologising to church members for "any pain, anxiety, disappointment, or grief that you have suffered because of me".[[55]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-55)

## Controversies

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Controversies")]

### Plagiarism

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Plagiarism")]

In March 2010, a blogger identified plagiarism on Kong Hee's _Daily Devotionals_ as they were similar to writings in another publication, _[The Leadership Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Leadership\_Bible?action=edit&redlink=1 "The Leadership Bible (page does not exist)")_ which had been published ten years prior. The copied text were published as physical copies into two books, _[Renewing Your Spiritual Energy in 90 Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renewing\_Your\_Spiritual\_Energy\_in\_90\_Days?action=edit&redlink=1 "Renewing Your Spiritual Energy in 90 Days (page does not exist)")_, without accreditation to the original authors. Kong Hee's daily devotionals were originally compiled from his personal reading notes and printed as supplementary reading for his members, free of charge. Some years later, due to popular demand overseas, a local publisher compiled and released foreign language translations of the devotional for sale.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Kong Hee posted a note on his website and explained that the devotion was "originally meant only for internal circulation among the members of my church. As such, there was an oversight in not quoting the sources of some portions that borrow from the writings of other Christian authors." There was also an apology for the oversight.[[56]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-56)[[57]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-ST-plagiarisedBook-57)

The publisher, who is also a member of City Harvest Church, acknowledged that at the time of publication, both himself and Mr Kong were aware that certain portions of the content were not original.[[57]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-ST-plagiarisedBook-57)[[58]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-58) The publisher of "Renewal" has since made amendments to the soft copies to include accreditation.

## Personal life

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kong_Hee&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Kong is married to pastor-turned-pop-singer [Ho Yeow Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ho_Yeow_Sun "Ho Yeow Sun"), also known as Sun Ho. They have one son, Dayan Kong, who was born in 2005.[[59]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-59)

Kong was the co-owner of a 5,242 sq ft duplex penthouse located on the 11th floor of The Oceanfront in the premium residential enclave [Sentosa Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentosa_Cove "Sentosa Cove"). The penthouse was co-owned with Indonesian tycoon Mr Wahju Hanafi, a church follower. The pair bought the penthouse for $9.33 million in 2007, each paying monthly installments of $17,000, before the apartment was sold at a loss of over S$2 million to a Kenyan diplomat.[[60]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kong_Hee#cite_note-60)
